title: Raloxifene -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Raloxifene is a medication used to treat postmenopausal osteoporosis and the risk reduction of invasive breast cancer in post-menopausal women. Osteoporosis represents an increased risk for developing fractures. Raloxifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator with an estrogen-agonistic effect on bone receptors. This activity outlines the indications, action, and contraindications of raloxifene as a valuable agent in the treatment of osteoporosis. In addition, this activity will highlight the mechanism of action, adverse event profile, and dosing pertinent for members of the interprofessional team in patients treated with raloxifene.

title: Raloxifene -- Continuing Education Activity

Review and select appropriate monitoring parameters for patients treated with raloxifene. Outline interprofessional team strategies for improving care coordination and communication for patients on raloxifene therapy where appropriate, including follow-up monitoring, and improve outcomes. title: Raloxifene -- Indications
content: Raloxifene is an FDA-approved second-generation selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that exerts estrogen-agonistic effects on bone, increasing bone mineral density and mass by decreasing bone resorption, and it is indicated for the treatment and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis. Raloxifene is also indicated for the reduction of risk of invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal women who are at high risk for invasive breast cancer or who have osteoporosis, with high risk defined as having 1 or more first-degree relatives with breast cancer, a prior breast biopsy demonstrating lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) or atypical hyperplasia, or a 5-year predicted breast cancer risk greater than 1.66%. [1] In addition, studies are currently underway investigating raloxifene as an adjuvant treatment for postmenopausal women with schizophrenia, with particularly promising results observed in individuals with mild presentations of the disorder. [2]

title: Raloxifene -- Mechanism of Action
content: The mechanism of action of raloxifene occurs through binding to estrogen receptors. This binding results in activation of estrogenic pathways (estrogen-agonistic effect) and blockade of estrogenic pathways (estrogen-antagonistic effect) in tissues that express estrogen receptors. These receptors are expressed as 2 isoforms: the alpha estrogen receptor (activating) and the beta estrogen receptor (inhibiting). Therefore, the expression of these receptors modifies cellular and tissue responses to estrogens.

title: Raloxifene -- Mechanism of Action
content: In postmenopausal osteoporosis, bone turnover dramatically increases. Bone resorption occurs at a faster rate than bone formation, leading to a progressive loss of bone mass and bone mineral density. This disease represents an elevated risk for developing fractures. Raloxifene can inhibit accelerated bone resorption both in the short term and in the long term, thereby increasing bone mineral density (BMD) and enhancing bone strength. Other pharmacologic agents for the management of osteoporosis are estrogen, bisphosphonates, selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs), parathyroid hormone (PTH), and calcium and vitamin D.

title: Raloxifene -- Mechanism of Action
content: It has an estrogen-antagonistic effect in the uterus and breast, in contrast with tamoxifen (a first-generation selective estrogen receptor modulator), which has an estrogen-agonistic effect on the uterus. In addition, raloxifene modifies cardiovascular risk markers by decreasing LDL-C, fibrinogen, and lipoprotein A, and increasing HDL2-C without modifying triglyceride levels. There are no recommendations for the use of raloxifene in BRCA1- or BRCA2-positive mutations; there are no reports of apparent effectiveness. This drug is not intended for use in treating patients with an established diagnosis of breast cancer. [3] [4]

title: Raloxifene -- Mechanism of Action
content: Raloxifene bioavailability is approximately 2%, with an absorption of 60%. The onset of action is 8 weeks, and distribution is mainly protein-bound (more than 95%). The drug is metabolized in the liver and is excreted primarily in feces (more than 93%) and urine (less than 0.2%).

title: Raloxifene -- Administration
content: Raloxifene hydrochloride is administered orally and is available as a 60 mg tablet. It is indicated for the treatment and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, with a recommended dose of 60 mg taken by mouth once daily. [5] For both prevention and treatment of osteoporosis, supplemental calcium and/or vitamin D should be added to the diet when daily intake is insufficient, as postmenopausal women require an average of 400–800 IU of vitamin D and 1,500 mg of elemental calcium daily; patients at high risk for vitamin D insufficiency, including those with gastrointestinal malabsorption syndromes, chronic illness, nursing home residence, or age greater than 70 years, may require additional vitamin D supplementation. Raloxifene is also prescribed for the prevention and risk reduction of invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal women at high risk for invasive breast cancer, with a recommended dose of 60 mg taken by mouth once daily for 5 years. [1] [6] Clinical trials have demonstrated additional benefits of raloxifene during menopause, including reductions in LDL cholesterol levels and decreased risk of pelvic organ prolapse and breast cancer. However, no effects on cognitive function, mood, or sleep disturbances have been reported. [7]

title: Raloxifene -- Administration -- Special Population
content: Patients with renal impairment: Use with caution; safety and efficacy are not well known in patients with moderate or severe renal impairment. Patients with liver impairment: Safety and efficacy are not well known in patients with hepatic impairment. [3] [8] Pregnancy and breastfeeding implications: Raloxifene is classified as pregnancy category X by the US FDA. Pregnancy and lactation constitute a contraindication to using raloxifene. Fertile women wishing to become pregnant need to avoid or discontinue this drug. It is not known whether raloxifene is excreted in human milk. Many medicines are excreted in human milk, so exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman.

title: Raloxifene -- Adverse Effects
content: Raloxifene's most common documented adverse effects are hot flashes, flu-like symptoms, muscle spasms, arthralgia, and infection. Less common effects are insomnia, vomiting, sinusitis, deep venous thrombosis, bronchitis, pharyngitis, and breast pain. [9] Raloxifene-treated women reported peripheral edema ( raloxifene 14.1% vs placebo 11.7%), muscle spasms/leg cramps (12.1% vs 8.3% ), hot flashes (7.8% vs 4.7% ), cholelithiasis (3.3% vs 2.6% ), and venous thromboembolic events 2.0% vs 1.4%).

title: Raloxifene -- Adverse Effects
content: The most serious adverse reaction related to raloxifene is venous thromboembolism (pulmonary embolism, deep venous thrombosis, and retinal vein thrombosis). During the clinical trial, with raloxifene treatment for 2.6 years, venous thromboembolism (VTE) precipitated in about 1 out of 100 patients. A total of 26 raloxifene-exposed women had a VTE compared to 11 placebo-treated women, and the highest risk of VTE was in the initial 4 months of the treatment phase with raloxifene.

title: Raloxifene -- Contraindications
content: Raloxifene has several important contraindications that clinicians should review carefully before prescribing. It should not be used in patients with a history of venous thromboembolism, including deep vein thrombosis, renal vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism, nor in those with active malignancy, current smoking, or known thrombophilic disorders such as factor V Leiden mutation, prothrombin gene mutation (G20210A), antiphospholipid syndrome, or deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C, or protein S.

title: Raloxifene -- Contraindications
content: Postmenopausal women with coronary heart disease or those at increased risk for coronary events have a higher risk of death due to stroke when treated with raloxifene. For this reason, a careful risk–benefit assessment is required in women with risk factors for stroke, including a history of transient ischemic attack (TIA) or stroke, cigarette smoking, hypertension, or atrial fibrillation.

title: Raloxifene -- Contraindications
content: Raloxifene should be used with caution in patients who are hospitalized, immobilized, unable to ambulate, or recovering from surgery, as these conditions further increase the risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. The safety of raloxifene in premenopausal women has not been established, and its use in this population is not recommended.

title: Raloxifene -- Contraindications -- Drug Interactions
content: There are reports of an interaction between ospemifene and raloxifene; it increases the effect of the other through synergism. Therefore, monitor the following drugs (for interaction with raloxifene) closely: apalutamide, cholestyramine, famciclovir, and levothyroxine. There is a reported minor interaction between raloxifene and warfarin; it increases the effect of warfarin by competing for plasma protein binding sites. [9] [10] Concomitant administration of raloxifene with amoxicillin, ampicillin, digoxin, corticosteroids, antacids, cholestyramine, other anion exchange resins, or systemic estrogens is not recommended. It should be used with caution with highly protein-bound drugs such as diazepam, diazoxide, and lidocaine, as it might affect the protein binding of other drugs.

title: Raloxifene -- Monitoring
content: Monitoring is recommended for patients with suggestive symptoms of deep vein thrombosis, including redness, tenderness, and inflammation of the calves and lower limbs. In such instances, patients should proceed immediately to the emergency department. A Doppler ultrasound of the lower limbs is indicated in the emergency department to rule out deep vein thrombosis. If such testing is positive, hospital admission is essential. In addition, it is vital to exclude pulmonary embolism in patients presenting with chest pain, shortness of breath, or hemoptysis.

title: Raloxifene -- Monitoring
content: Reports recommend suspending raloxifene for 72 hours before and during expected patient immobilization. When raloxifene is administered concomitantly with warfarin or other warfarin derivatives, monitor prothrombin time more closely when initiating or discontinuing raloxifene. Supplementation with vitamin D and calcium is also recommended in conjunction with raloxifene therapy. In addition, monitor hepatic profile and triglyceride levels, given estrogen's agonistic effect on triglyceride levels.

title: Raloxifene -- Monitoring
content: Monitor for any unexpected abnormal uterine bleeding. For patients with abnormal uterine bleeding in using raloxifene, it is recommended to establish a consultation with OB/GYN and initiate further workup to establish the source of the bleeding. An endometrial biopsy is suggested to rule out endometrial cancer. [10] Investigations and research have examined the effects of raloxifene on the heart, given its estrogen-agonistic action at the heart's estrogen receptors. Reports indicate that raloxifene does not produce myocardial hypertrophy in postmenopausal women after being treated for 6 months. [11] [12]

title: Raloxifene -- Toxicity
content: There is some documentation of increased risk of deep vein thrombosis, embolic cerebrovascular accident, and pulmonary embolism with the usage of this drug. Patients developing new-onset vaginal bleeding require a workup, including an endometrial biopsy and an OB/GYN consultation. There are some reports of an increased risk of death due to a cerebrovascular accident in trials of postmenopausal women with coronary heart disease or with high-risk factors for coronary arterial disease. [4] [12]

title: Raloxifene -- Toxicity
content: In an 8-week clinical study, 63 postmenopausal women safely tolerated 600 mg raloxifene daily. No death associated with raloxifene overdose has been reported in postmarketing spontaneous reports. One patient overdosed on raloxifene, 1.5 grams, was reported. Adverse reactions (mainly leg cramps and dizziness) were reported in approximately half of the adults who took more than 180 mg of raloxifene. Overdose toxicity was reported with 180 mg raloxifene in 2 18-month-old children. Reported adverse reactions include vomiting, ataxia, diarrhea, dizziness, rash, flushing, tremor, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. There is no specific antidote for raloxifene.

title: Raloxifene -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Raloxifene can be prescribed by primary care clinicians, OB/GYNs, and endocrinologists. The drug is useful for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis and the prevention of breast cancer. However, healthcare workers, including pharmacists, must warn the patient that the drug can cause deep vein thrombosis and explain how to detect symptoms and present to the emergency department immediately. Also, the drug can cause hot flashes, flu-like symptoms, and muscle spasms. The interprofessional team should work together to monitor the patient closely for deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, or embolic cerebrovascular accident. Patient education should include immediate notification of the provider if shortness of breath, chest pain, arm or leg weakness, calf redness, or calf pain. Nursing staff must be vigilant in asking about these symptoms at every follow-up visit and alerting the prescriber to any concerns. The pharmacist also needs to perform medication reconciliation to avoid drug interactions and verify that all dosing is appropriate. A provider may want these medications stopped before prolonged bed rest, immobility, or surgery. [12] [5] Prescribing raloxifene and follow-up monitoring require an interprofessional team approach, including clinicians, specialists, nurses, specialty-trained nurses, and pharmacists, who collaborate across disciplines to achieve optimal patient outcomes and prevent complications.
